chunks: Muhammad ibn Ja'far Al-Razzaz Al-Kufi narrated to me from his uncle Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, from Musa ibn Sa'dan, from Abdullah ibn al-Qasim, from Umar ibn Aban al-Kalbi, from Aban ibn Taghlib, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: There are four thousand angels by the grave of al-Husayn (peace be upon him), disheveled and covered with dust, weeping for him until the Day of Judgment. Their chief is an angel named Mansur. No visitor comes to visit him but they receive him, and no one bids him farewell but they accompany him. No one falls ill but they visit him, and no one dies but they pray over him [and over his funeral] and seek forgiveness for him after his death.

key_terms.شُعْثٌ غُبْرٌ: Disheveled and covered with dust, indicating a state of perpetual mourning

ai.seo_question: What do the angels do at the grave of Imam al-Husayn (peace be upon him)?
ai.summary: This hadith from Ibn Qulawayh’s *Kamil al-Ziyarat* highlights the cosmological significance of Karbala, portraying the grave of Imam al-Husayn (a.s.) as a spiritual hub where four thousand angels, led by Mansur, maintain eternal vigil. Their continuous weeping underscores the enduring sorrow of the Ahl al-Bayt, while their active engagement with visitors—welcoming, bidding farewell, and interceding for the ill and deceased—emphasizes the reciprocal spiritual benefits of Ziyarah in Shia tradition.
